1:
Adam Clarke assigns the opening question to the bride’s companions, and notes that the Hebrew and all the versions join the verse to the preceding chapter. Keil and Delitzsch supply the setting: the longing survives her waking as the after-effect of the dream, and in the morning she meets the daughters of Jerusalem, who having made her describe her friend now ask which way he turned, so that they may seek him with her. John Gill notes only that the title they give her is the one used before, and by Christ before them, repeated to show the question is serious.

Matthew Henry makes the enquiry the turning point. The women who had earlier asked what her beloved was more than another are now in love with him themselves, and he gives two reasons: she had shown them his excellencies, so that though they have not seen him they believe and therefore love, since those who undervalue Christ do so because they do not know him; and she had expressed her own love and triumphed in it, so that the flame in her breast scattered sparks into theirs, pious zeal spreading as sinful desire does. Henry concedes what the request would otherwise be: as a merely human exchange it would be an indecent compliment, since love is jealous of a rival; taken spiritually it is the opposite, for those who truly love Christ want others to love him too, and the greatest respect the church’s children can show their mother is to join her in seeking him.

Her answer sends them to a garden, variously located. Gill offers a literal setting first: the king was said to go out very early in great pomp to a pleasant place two miles from the city, abounding in gardens and water, or to the royal gardens below the palace, so that going down is exact. He then reads the descent as the low estate of God’s people and the condescension of one who visits them there. John Wesley allegorizes it steadily: the garden is the church at large and the gardens and beds its assemblies, the spices are the gifts and graces of the Spirit, the feeding is his own refreshment, and the lilies are either believers gathered to him or the prayers and praises of his people in public congregations. Keil and Delitzsch treat her answer as an inference, since she reasons from what her beloved likes to where he must be.

Henry keeps the garden enclosed and separated from the world, and draws the rule that those who would find Christ must attend him in his ordinances, the word, sacraments and prayer. The gathering of lilies he turns toward death: a believer’s death is no more than the owner of a garden plucking a favourite flower, which he preserves from withering.

The mutual claim is read as a confession of faith. Gill says her interest in Christ held through all her unbecoming behaviour, and reports a Jewish commentator who joins the words to the last verse, so the sense becomes, though he is gone and I am left alone, I know I am his and he is mine — a reading Gill thinks throws a beauty on the words, since the glory of faith is to believe in an unseen Christ, though he allows she may by now have found him and speak as the doubting apostle did. Keil and Delitzsch observe that she never calls him her husband but always her beloved and her friend, love here being viewed as far as possible apart from its basis in the animal nature, and that the description hovers between the clothed and the unclothed in a way that suits the mystical reading. Henry ends where the verse does: if our hearts witness that we are his, we need not question his being ours, since the covenant never breaks on his side.
4:
The first name in the praise starts a dispute about dating. John Gill allows that Tirzah might be the name of some beautiful woman well known at the time, since one of the daughters of Zelophehad bore it; but he prefers a city, since the next clause names Jerusalem for the same reason, a place once held by an ancient king of Canaan and later by Jeroboam and his successors. Adam Clarke puts it in Ephraim, the residence of Jeroboam before Samaria was built, its name signifying delightful, and says the poet compares the bride to the two finest places in the land, the capitals of the two kingdoms. Matthew Henry places the same city in Manasseh, glosses the name as pleasant, and dwells rather on Jerusalem, which the king had built and beautified and whose greatest beauty was that it was holy.

Charles Ellicott sees no reason for naming Tirzah beside Jerusalem except that both were capitals, north and south, and takes that to fix the date of the poem within limits; he traces the northern seat of government from Shechem to Penuel beyond the Jordan and then to Tirzah, formerly held by a petty Canaanite prince and a capital only until the reign of Omri. He adds that the Greek and Latin versions turn the name into a word for pleasantness. Keil and Delitzsch report the same inference, that the prominence of Tirzah puts the Song after the division of the kingdom and its author in the north, but keep the traditional authorship themselves, and read the verse as the king measuring her beauty by the chief cities of his kingdom.

The last clause divides them. Henry takes the terror as the church’s own: censures duly administered strike an awe on men’s consciences, the word casts down imaginations, and even an unbeliever is convinced by the solemnity of holy ordinances. John Wesley keeps it simpler: she is terrible to her enemies, whom God will certainly destroy. Clarke looks for the picture behind it and finds the caravans of the East, which travel by night divided into companies, each known by the shape of the brazier carried on a long pole at its head, some holding ten or twelve lights and cut into different forms so that a pilgrim knows his own company; a caravan of many thousands so divided must make a splendid and even a terrible appearance. Gill hears the speech as a return from silence, the beloved unable to refrain longer, like another Joseph, since for all her behaviour she was his love still.

Asking her to turn her eyes away is read three ways. Keil and Delitzsch derive the verb from a root meaning to press impetuously against someone, and take the intensive form as pressing overpoweringly and infusing a paralyzing terror, one old version rendering it to put to flight. Ellicott resists that: the root idea is rather to show spirit against oppression, so the form should mean make me spirited or bold, though he grants that the Greek and Latin, and many moderns after them, take it as scare or dazzle. Clarke joins his own image to that sense: after the dazzle of so many fires the eye cannot bear the sight, and her look pierced the heart of whoever met it. Gill will not have dislike in it but the opposite, a man ravished and unable to hold out longer; and he reports a rendering that turns the words about, so that she is asked to look him full in the face, having hung her head in shame at their first meeting since her unkindness. Wesley reads it as a poetical way of saying how beautiful the church was in his eyes, and calls the repetition of the lines on her hair and teeth from an earlier chapter not vain but a confirmation that her miscarriage had not alienated his affection.
7:
John Gill says the descriptions are repeated to confirm the beauty and show it unchanged despite her failings; and he notices what is missing: the clause about her lips and speech is left out here, added at the end by the Greek version but absent from the Hebrew copies and unnoticed in the Targum.

The court is counted differently by each. Gill defines the three ranks — queens the lawful wives, concubines secondary wives whose children did not inherit, and virgins maids of honour in attendance — and allows the verse to be read as an assertion or a supposition, taking the allusion from the custom of kings, or from a nuptial solemnity. Charles Ellicott finds the numbers far more sober than the historical books give, and suggests the larger figures mark a later form of the traditions about the court, this poetic version being truer; he also settles a word, since pairing the term for maidens with that for concubines decides for girls rather than virgins. Adam Clarke puts the verse into the bridegroom’s mouth as a concession — though there be sixty queens and eighty concubines and countless virgins, thou art the One in whom I delight beyond all — and John Wesley takes the number as a certain one standing for an uncertain, none of the beautiful women in the courts of princes being comparable to her.

What the oneness means is the chief dispute. Gill offers two senses: the small number of the church against the nations, like one to sixty or eighty, or her unity, a single body of many members actuated by one Spirit and having one Head; and where other princes have many, this one had a single spouse and desired no other. Ellicott calls the verse a eulogy on monogamy, which he says was in practice always the rule among the Jews, the exceptions lying only with kings and the very rich, and adds that the praise is sharpened by putting that testimony into the mouths of the queens and concubines themselves. Keil and Delitzsch attend to the question that follows, noting that the same words were asked earlier of the woman being brought to the king, whereas here they are asked of one who moves in what is his as her own, and that the verb of looking forth properly means to bend forward, since one leans out to look. Wesley makes the only one a comparison with an only child, as dear to a parent as such children are. Clarke reports that the queens and concubines praised her as the most accomplished of her sex, and marks the verse as the end of the fourth night of the marriage week.

The closing question is answered with light. Clarke ranks the images by brightness: lovely as the dawn, more resplendent as the moon, and beyond that clear and bright as the sun, yet dangerous to look at, formidable as the lights carried at the head of every company in a great caravan; and he adds that comparing a beautiful woman to an unclouded full moon recurs continually in the Asiatic poets. Ellicott assigns the words to the admiring ladies, argues that the paragraph break belongs at the next verse, and compares the lines in which Juliet is called the sun, observing that the poet joins both great lights to the dawn and puts the praise in the mouths of the lesser beauties of the night, who feel their inferiority when the moon rises and more still before the sun. Gill supplies a word of saying to connect the question with what precedes, gathers parallels from a Greek poet who gives the dawn rosy fingers, a saffron garment and a golden throne; then he turns the gradations of light into the ages of the church. Wesley keeps to the speakers and their wonder at how excellent a person this is.
11:
John Gill starts from a custom, that newly married people threw nuts among children for pastime, as a sign of renouncing childish things. He rejects nutmegs, which did not grow in those parts, and prefers walnuts, the word being the one the Arabs use; the nuts he reads as believers, of mean outward appearance but valuable within. Adam Clarke guesses at the almond rather than the hazel, and takes this verse and the next to concern the consummation of the marriage; but he cautions that the circumstances are so interwoven and displaced that it is exceedingly difficult to arrange them or say who is speaking, though other writers find no difficulty because they have a system, and the system explains everything.

Matthew Henry uses the verse to explain the withdrawal. Even out of sight he was no further off than the garden, hidden among its trees in a low valley, observing how the vine flourished so that he might promote its flourishing; Christ marks the first beginnings of grace and the early buddings of devout affection, and is as pleased with them as we are with the blossoms of spring.

The chariots divide them. Gill allows either, since the opening clause may be rendered I know not: on one reading the church, not knowing where he had gone, ran after him as swiftly as those chariots and with a driver’s courage in battle. Henry gives the verse to Christ and makes it the moment of return, when he could no longer keep at a distance, his repentings kindled by her lamentation and languishing desire, so that he resolved at once to fly back. Wesley reads it the same way, a vehement desire for the spouse, understood figuratively so as to agree with the majesty and omniscience of Christ, and supposes the name that of an eminent charioteer known for speed. Keil and Delitzsch make her soul, that is her love, the thing that raised her to the royal chariots of her people, where she sits beside the king who drives; she knew it and did not know it, being neither elated by it nor ashamed of her origin. Clarke declines the allegory: the chariots were probably proverbial for speed, the passage marks a strong agitation of mind like what we call palpitation of the heart, and since he sees no spiritual meaning he asks to be excused from commenting on anything but the letter.

The fourfold call is felt by everyone. Keil and Delitzsch have the daughters, emboldened by her unassuming answer, entreating her earnestly and even with tears as she walks from the garden to the palace, the verb of looking meaning to sink oneself into a thing by gazing; and here for the first time, they note, she is addressed by name. Clarke derives that name as a feminine formed from the king’s, on the pattern by which Charlotte is formed from Charles or Janette from John, and takes the address to be made to her as the acknowledged wife. Gill reaches the same by way of custom, since a wife took her husband’s name, and adds that the root carries both perfection and peace, neither of them hers in herself. Wesley hears in the repetition both a passionate love and her backwardness, since she who had pursued him when he was gone was ready to wander now that he was coming.

The closing image is left unsettled. Clarke offers the musicians of the camps, or the choirs of the bride’s virgins and the bridegroom’s companions, admits the likeness is not very perceptible, reports a paraphrase making them the camps of two kingdoms, and concludes that the best conjectures afford little satisfaction. Wesley takes the one spouse to be the whole multitude of believers and the two armies confederate, signifying a union of peoples and the strength of a church drawn up like a host.
